title: A Man for All Seasons: The Playwright and the History Behind the Play
summary: Robert Bolt, the 'King's Great Matter', the break with Rome, the Act of Supremacy and the oath, and who Sir Thomas More was.

p: Robert Bolt (1924 to 1995) was an English playwright and screenwriter, famous for historical drama. He was not writing as a historian but as a moralist: he used real people to explore universal questions of conscience, honesty and corruption.

Time: England in the 1530s. King: Henry VIII. The 'King's Great Matter': Henry was married to Catherine of Aragon, who had given him a daughter, Mary, but no son. He believed the marriage was cursed and wanted to marry Anne Boleyn.

The problem: England was a Catholic country, and only the Pope could cancel the marriage. For political reasons, the Pope refused. The 'solution': Henry broke away from the Catholic Church. Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, which made the King, not the Pope, the supreme head of the Church in England.

The oath: to enforce the change, important people (bishops, lawyers, officials) had to swear an oath accepting it. To swear was to save your life but, for a devout Catholic, to betray God. To refuse was to risk death for treason. (A historical note: in real history, More was first asked to take an oath connected with the Act of Succession, which confirmed the new marriage, and the charge of denying the King's supremacy was brought at his trial. The play joins these events into one test of conscience.)

More was a real person: a brilliant lawyer, a devout Catholic and a humanist (a Renaissance scholar). He was Lord Chancellor of England, the highest officer of the kingdom after the King, and was a personal friend of Henry. His problem is that he is loyal to his King but loyal to God first. He cannot and will not swear the oath. The title comes from a description of More as a man who could adapt to every season (every circumstance) of life without giving up his principles.

Physical: sixteenth-century London: More's home in Chelsea (a place of warmth, family and ideas), Hampton Court (the palace of power) and the Tower of London (the prison). Atmosphere: it changes from political intrigue and lively debate to fear, suspicion and danger.

title: A Man for All Seasons: The Story of the Two Acts
summary: The events of Act One and Act Two: Rich, Cromwell, More's resignation, his silence, the trial and the perjury.

p: We meet Sir Thomas More, witty, moral and happy with his family: his wife Alice, his daughter Meg and her suitor Roper. We meet Richard Rich, a young, ambitious man looking for a post. More does not trust him and suggests a safe, honest job as a teacher. Rich is insulted; he wants power.

We meet Thomas Cromwell, the practical, ruthless politician who is helping the King to get his divorce. Cardinal Wolsey, the old Chancellor, fails to get the divorce from the Pope and falls in disgrace. The King makes More Chancellor, hoping that More's honest name will help his cause. The Act of Supremacy is passed. More cannot support it and tries to resign; the King is furious. More falls from power. He is now a private citizen, but he is not safe.

More is poor but firm. His defence is silence: if he says nothing against the King's Act, the law cannot touch him. Cromwell is determined to break him and 'invites' him for questioning to trap him into speaking. More says nothing.
His family is frightened. They beg him to say the words of the oath even if he does not mean them. He refuses, explaining that his conscience is his 'self'.

The betrayal: Cromwell has Rich arrested on a false charge and offers him a deal: give false evidence against More and become powerful. The trial (the climax): More defends himself brilliantly, using the law, and seems about to be acquitted. Then Rich is called to the stand and lies under oath (perjury), swearing that he heard More deny the King's supremacy. More is found guilty.
The end: More is executed, saying that he dies as the King's good servant, but God's first.

Exposition: More's home and the problem of the divorce. Rising action: the Act of Supremacy; More's resignation; Cromwell's pressure. Climax: the trial and Rich's lie. Falling action: the sentence and the farewell to his family. Resolution: the execution.

title: A Man for All Seasons: Themes, Characters and Style
summary: Conscience and the State, identity as 'self', corruption by ambition, law and silence; the main characters including the Common Man; and Bolt's Brechtian style.

p: 1. Conscience and integrity against duty to the State (the central theme): More puts conscience first; Cromwell, Rich and Norfolk put loyalty to the King and to the State first. The play asks what a person should do when the law of the country is wrong.

2. Identity and the 'self': More says that when a man takes an oath he holds himself in his own hands like water, and if he opens his fingers he cannot hope to find himself again. To swear against his conscience would be a kind of death of his true self.

3. Corruption by ambition: Rich begins as an ambitious job-seeker, tells small lies and ends by giving false evidence to become Attorney-General for Wales. More's famous remark, that it profits a man nothing to give his soul for the whole world but for Wales, shows how cheaply Rich sold himself.
4. Law, justice and silence: More loves the law as a fortress that protects society; the tragedy is that Cromwell uses the same law as a weapon.
Sir Thomas More: a man of complete integrity but not a plaster saint; he is witty, sharp, a fine lawyer and afraid of death, which makes his stand more heroic.
Thomas Cromwell: the antagonist and 'modern man'; practical, efficient and without scruple; he is the opposite of More.
Richard Rich: a weak man with no core, who wants power; a smaller villain than Cromwell, but his lie kills More.

The Common Man: an actor who plays many small roles (More's steward, a boatman, a jailer, the jury foreman). He stands for ordinary people who 'do not want trouble', and the play suggests that this apathy allows evil to happen; as the jury, he finds More guilty.

Historical drama: a real event used to explore timeless moral questions. The alienation effect (from the German playwright Bertolt Brecht): the Common Man speaks directly to the audience and changes costume on stage. This reminds us that we are watching a play and keeps us thinking instead of simply feeling. Bolt wants us to ask: 'What would I have done?'

Rich is the clearest example of corruption by ambition. In his first scene he is eager for a position and rejects More's honest advice. By the end he lies under oath to destroy the man who tried to help him, and in return he gets high office. His fall shows how a person can be corrupted one small compromise at a time.

sections.h: Law as shield and as weapon
p: More sees the law as a shield: if he stays silent, the law protects him. Cromwell sees it as a weapon: he can twist it, buy witnesses and use it to destroy an enemy. The conflict between these two views is the heart of the play.

title: An Inspector Calls: The Playwright, Setting and Story
summary: J. B. Priestley, why 1945 and 1912 matter, and the story of the three acts from the dinner party to the final telephone call.

p: J. B. Priestley (1894 to 1984) was a British novelist, broadcaster and playwright, and a committed socialist who was deeply concerned with inequality and the class system. His play is a 'morality play': a play with a strong moral message.

The play was written in 1945, after two world wars, when Britain was being rebuilt and the old class system was breaking down. Priestley wanted a fairer, more equal society. It is set in 1912, before the wars, in the comfortable home of a wealthy upper-middle-class family, the Birlings, who feel no responsibility for others. Setting the play in 1912 lets the audience in 1945 see how wrong the confident attitudes of that time were. The play is a parable: a simple story that teaches a lesson about social responsibility.

The Birling family (Arthur, Sybil, their daughter Sheila and son Eric) and Sheila's fiancé Gerald Croft are having a dinner party to celebrate the engagement. Mr Birling lectures them on 'minding your own business' and looking after yourself. He says the Titanic is unsinkable and that there will be no war: ideas that the 1945 audience knows are wrong (dramatic irony).

An Inspector Goole arrives. A young working-class woman, Eva Smith, has died at the infirmary after drinking disinfectant. Part 1: Mr Birling dismissed her from his factory two years before as a ringleader of a strike for higher wages. Part 2: Sheila had her dismissed from a shop out of jealousy and bad temper. Sheila is horrified and accepts her guilt.

Part 3: Eva, calling herself Daisy Renton, was Gerald's mistress for a summer; he then left her. Part 4: Mrs Birling, who heads a women's charity, refused help to a pregnant Eva who came to her, and says the father of the child alone is to blame.

Part 5: the father was Eric. He had a drunken affair with her, got her pregnant and stole money from his father's office to help her. The chain is complete: each of them gave a 'push'. The Inspector warns that 'we are members of one body', and if people will not learn this, they will be taught it 'in fire and blood and anguish'. He leaves.

Twist 1: the family finds that there is no Inspector Goole on the police force. Twist 2: no girl has died at the infirmary that night. The older Birlings and Gerald feel relieved and laugh it off. The younger generation, Sheila and Eric, say that what they did is just as bad. Final twist: the telephone rings; a girl has just died after drinking disinfectant, and a police inspector is on his way.

p: Many readers hear in 'Goole' the word 'ghoul', a spirit, which suggests that the Inspector is more than a policeman. Who is he? A real person? A ghost? A conscience? A time traveller? The play leaves it open, and you may offer your own theory with reasons.

Priestley shows two attitudes. The parents are set in their ways and cannot learn. The children are open to change and feel responsibility. Priestley places his hope for a better society in the young.

Sheila begins as a spoilt young woman who enjoys the engagement ring. When the Inspector exposes her part in Eva's dismissal, she is the first to accept blame. In the final scene she refuses to pretend that nothing has happened. This change shows that people can learn and grow, which is Priestley's message.

title: An Inspector Calls: Themes and Dramatic Techniques
summary: Social responsibility, class, the generation gap and hypocrisy, together with the well-made play, the unities, dramatic irony, the cyclical ending and the morality play.

p: 1. Social (collective) responsibility: the central theme. The play attacks the idea of 'every man for himself' and shows that the Birlings' private acts had public and fatal results.

2. Social class: the Birlings feel superior to Eva Smith, whom they used and discarded: cheap labour (Mr Birling), dismissal out of spite (Sheila), sexual use (Gerald and Eric) and refused help (Mrs Birling). The play exposes the hypocrisy of the 'respectable' upper classes.
3. Old and young: the old are 'static' and unteachable; the young are 'dynamic' and open to change.
4. Hypocrisy: the family cares about its public image but hides secrets and cruelty.
The 'well-made play': a tightly built plot rising to a climax; Priestley uses it and then surprises us with supernatural twists.

The three unities (a classical idea): one action (the investigation), one place (the Birlings' dining room) and one stretch of time (about two hours, in real time). This makes the play tense and shuts the characters in with the Inspector's questions.

Dramatic irony: the audience knows more than the character; when Mr Birling declares that the Titanic is unsinkable and there will be no war, the audience of 1945 knows he is wrong, so they doubt everything else he says.
The Inspector as a device: he starts the 'chain of events', controls the order of the questioning and leaves.
Cyclical structure: the ending returns to the beginning; the second telephone call announces another inspection. It gives the characters and the audience a second chance.

sections.h: A morality play for modern times
p: A medieval morality play showed an 'Everyman' visited by figures such as Death or Good Deeds who taught him a lesson. In this play the Birling family is 'Everyman' (every family) and the Inspector is a character like Conscience who comes to teach: we are all members of one body.

sections.h: Model answer: the three unities and the atmosphere
p: Because the play happens in one room, in real time and about one subject, there is no escape for the characters. The audience feels the pressure of the questioning and cannot look away. This builds suspense and makes the moral message hard to avoid.

activity: Write two paragraphs agreeing or disagreeing with this statement: 'The real crime is not what the Birlings did but their refusal to accept responsibility.' Explain the cyclical structure and the three unities.

o: The audience knows more than a character

sections.h: A quick review of the poems
p: Okara: loss of sincerity; Soyinka: the power of the night; Osundare: political apathy (link to the Inspector's message that we are all responsible); Cheney-Coker: memory and the sea; Afriyie-Vidza: a tested love or life; Kamara: a new language; Angelou: resilience; Byron: harmony of inner and outer beauty; Heaney: heritage and the craft of writing; Adcock: expectation and reality.

Compare Ananse and Sir Thomas More: both are clever, but one uses cunning and the other uses the law and his conscience. Compare the 'villains': the greedy chiefs, Cromwell and Rich, and the Birlings. Which play has the clearest moral message, and which the most ambiguous? How do the Storyteller and the Common Man both break the fourth wall, and why? How does the theme of 'Not My Business' connect to 'An Inspector Calls'?

sections.h: Essay plan: morality and justice in two plays
p: Introduction: say what you mean by moral and legal justice. Paragraph 1: justice in the first play (for example in Anansewa, the funeral tests the chiefs and rewards honour, but Ananse is not punished). Paragraph 2: justice in the second play (for example in A Man for All Seasons, the law condemns an honest man, so legal justice and moral justice separate). Paragraph 3: compare them. Conclusion: your own judgement.
Read each play, not only the notes. Learn two short quotations and one key scene for each. Know the stage terms: fourth wall, episodic structure, dramatic irony, alienation effect, unities.
